subtitle: The gateway to the Microsoft cloud. Cloud concepts, Azure architecture and services, governance and management. Structured in 3 main domains, following the official Microsoft skills outline (updated January 14, 2026).

section1.lead: AZ-900 is the Azure Fundamentals certification — the first step into any Microsoft cloud career. It measures conceptual knowledge: you don't need to know how to configure services, but you must know what each one does, when to use it, and how they relate to one another.
section1.format_value: Online (proctored) or Pearson VUE testing center
section1.domain1_desc: models, service types, benefits. The theoretical foundation.
section1.domain2_desc: the heart of the exam: regions, compute, networking, storage, identity, security.
section1.callout_text: Study in domain order — they were designed in a logical sequence. Concepts first, then services (which use those concepts), then governance (which manages the services). Skipping steps causes confusion.
section1.free_practice_text: Microsoft offers a free official practice assessment for AZ-900 inside Learn — works as a thermometer before booking the paid exam.

section2.lead: Before talking about Azure, you must understand what the cloud is. These concepts apply to any provider (AWS, GCP, Azure) — and Microsoft tests exactly this vocabulary in this domain.
section2.compute_p1: Cloud computing is the delivery of IT services (compute, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet. Instead of buying servers, you rent capacity as you use it, with elastic scale and consumption-based billing.
section2.shared_resp_intro: The shared responsibility model defines what the provider (Microsoft) handles and what the customer handles. Always the customer's: identities and accounts, devices, data, access management.
section2.shared_resp_d1: Provider: hardware, physical network, virtualization. Customer: OS, runtime, application, data, identity.
section2.shared_resp_d2: Provider: everything up through OS and runtime. Customer: application, data, identity.
section2.shared_resp_d3: Provider: pretty much everything. Customer: data, identity, app configuration.
section2.public_desc: provider's infrastructure, accessible over the internet. Cheaper, more scalable, less control. E.g., public Azure, AWS.
section2.private_desc: infrastructure dedicated to one organization (on-premises or hosted). More control, more expensive, limited scale.
section2.hybrid_desc: combines public and private cloud with connectivity. Lets you keep sensitive workloads on-premises and use the cloud for the rest.
section2.multi_desc: simultaneous use of more than one public cloud (e.g., Azure + AWS). Reduces lock-in, increases complexity.
section2.consumption_p1: Cloud uses the OpEx (operating expense) model — you pay as you consume, with no upfront capital investment. Traditional on-premises is CapEx (capital expense) — you buy equipment upfront.
section2.pricing_d1: Pay only for what you use, per minute/second. Maximum flexibility, highest price.
section2.pricing_d2: Commit to 1 or 3 years. Up to 72% discount vs pay-as-you-go.
section2.pricing_d3: Uses Azure's spare capacity. Up to 90% discount, but can be interrupted at any time. Good for interruption-tolerant workloads.
section2.pricing_d4: Commit to a fixed hourly amount for 1 or 3 years. More flexible than reserved — applies across multiple compute types.
section2.serverless_p1: Serverless does not mean there's no server — it means you don't manage the server. The provider scales automatically; you pay only for execution. Azure examples: Azure Functions, Logic Apps.
section2.serverless_d1: Auto-scale (from zero to thousands of executions), pay-per-execution, no server to provision or maintain, ideal for event-driven workloads.
section2.benefit_avail_d: Typical SLA of 99.9% or higher. Multiple datacenters, automatic redundancy.
section2.benefit_scale_d: Vertical (increase VM resources) or horizontal (add more VMs). Can be manual or automatic.
section2.benefit_elastic_d: Resources scale up and down automatically with demand. Black Friday: scales out; Sunday night: shrinks.
section2.benefit_reliab_d: Ability to recover from failures. Regional failover, geographic replication.
section2.benefit_predict_d: Predictable performance (autoscale) and predictable costs (planning, Cost Management, alerts).
section2.benefit_sec_d: Physical layers, identity controls, encryption in transit and at rest, certified compliance.
section2.benefit_gov_d: Centralized policies, RBAC, audit logs, inherited standards via management groups.
section2.benefit_manage_d: Web portal, CLI, PowerShell, REST APIs, templates, automation. Of the cloud (autoscale) and in the cloud (you managing resources).
section2.iaas_desc: You rent virtual machines, networks, storage. The provider handles physical hardware and virtualization. You manage OS, patches, runtime, app. More flexible, more responsibility.
section2.iaas_uses: Use cases: lift-and-shift of on-premises VMs, dev/test, hosting legacy apps, fine-grained OS control.
section2.iaas_examples: Azure examples: Virtual Machines, Virtual Network, Disks.
section2.paas_desc: You focus on code and data. The provider handles OS, runtime, patches, scaling. You don't see the underlying VM. More productive, less low-level control.
section2.paas_uses: Use cases: developing and deploying web apps, APIs, microservices; managed databases; workloads where you want to focus on code.
section2.paas_examples: Azure examples: App Service, Azure SQL Database, Azure Functions, AKS.
section2.saas_desc: Complete software delivered over the internet, by subscription. Customer just uses it. Provider handles everything — infra, software, updates.
section2.saas_uses: Use cases: productivity (email, doc editing), CRM, ERP. For the customer, it's just sign in and use.
section2.tip_html: Shared responsibility: identity and data are always the customer's. OpEx vs CapEx: cloud is OpEx. Lift-and-shift = IaaS; new code = PaaS; end-user app = SaaS.

section3.lead: This is the largest domain of the exam. Here you must know service names, when to use each, and how they relate hierarchically. Microsoft tests vocabulary heavily.
section3.regions_topic: Regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
section3.regions_p1: A region is a set of geographically close datacenters connected by a low-latency network. Azure has over 60 regions worldwide. You choose the region for your resources (usually the closest to users or based on legal requirements).
section3.regions_p2: Region pairs: each region has a paired region in the same country (or continent). Pairs are at least 500 km apart and receive updates sequentially (not simultaneously). Some geo-redundancy options use the pair automatically. E.g., Brazil South ↔ South Central US (cross-continent pair, an exception).
section3.regions_p3: Sovereign regions: isolated environments separate from public regions for government customers or countries with specific requirements. Examples: Azure Government (US), Azure China (operated by 21Vianet), Azure Germany.
section3.az_text: Physically separated datacenters within a region, each with independent power, cooling, and network. Typically 3 zones per region. Zone-redundant resources survive a full zone failure.
section3.dc_text: Physical buildings with servers, networking, and cooling. The customer never interacts directly — always via region/zone. Multiple datacenters make up a region.
section3.hierarchy_lead: Hierarchy, from broadest to most specific:
section3.hierarchy_l1: Management groups — aggregate multiple subscriptions to apply policies and RBAC at scale.
section3.hierarchy_l2: Subscriptions — billing and limit boundary. Each subscription has an owner, quotas, and separate billing.
section3.hierarchy_l3: Resource groups — logical containers for related resources (a whole app, for instance). A resource can only be in one group, but it can be moved.
section3.hierarchy_l4: Resources — VMs, databases, networks, storage accounts. The billable units.
section3.vm_desc: IaaS. You choose OS, size, disk. Maximum control, maximum responsibility. Ideal for lift-and-shift and workloads needing specific OS.
section3.vmss_desc: Sets of identical VMs that scale together, with load balancing. Grows and shrinks automatically.
section3.as_desc: Group VMs to ensure SLA even during maintenance. Distributes VMs across fault domains (racks) and update domains. SLA 99.95%.
section3.avd_desc: Virtualization of Windows desktops and apps in the cloud. Access from any device. Good for remote workforce and BYOD.
section3.container_desc: A Docker container without needing to manage a VM or orchestrator. Good for short, isolated tasks.
section3.aks_desc: Managed Kubernetes for orchestrating containers at scale. Azure manages the control plane.
section3.functions_desc: Serverless. You write a function, define the trigger (HTTP, queue, timer), Azure runs it. Pay only for execution.
section3.appservice_desc: PaaS for web apps, APIs, mobile backends. Supports multiple runtimes. Vertical and horizontal scale. Deployment slots.
section3.hosting_p1: Summary of when to pick each option to host an application:
section3.hosting_l1: VMs: maximum control, legacy app, specific OS requirements.
section3.hosting_l2: App Service (Web Apps): modern web app or API, without managing OS. Reasonable default for most.
section3.hosting_l3: Containers (ACI, AKS): portability across environments, microservices, fine-grained scale.
section3.hosting_l4: Functions: light event-driven logic, pay only per execution.
section3.vnet_desc: Private cloud network, isolated. Define your own IP ranges, subnets, route tables.
section3.subnet_desc: Segmentations within the VNet. Let you separate tiers (web, app, db) and apply different rules to each.
section3.peering_desc: Connects two VNets — same or different regions. Traffic stays on Microsoft's private backbone.
section3.dns_desc: Hosts DNS domains in Azure. Fast resolution, integrated with the portal and CLI.
section3.vpn_desc: Connects your on-premises network to Azure over encrypted internet (IPsec). Site-to-site, point-to-site.
section3.er_desc: Dedicated private connection between on-premises and Azure (does not traverse the public internet). Higher bandwidth, lower latency.
section3.endpoints_text: Public endpoint: service accessible from the internet (with a public IP). Private endpoint: the service gets an IP from your VNet — accessible only inside the network, without crossing the public internet. Increases security.
section3.blob_desc: Unstructured objects — images, videos, backups, logs. Large volumes. Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive tiers.
section3.files_desc: Managed SMB and NFS file shares. Replaces traditional file servers. Mountable on Windows, Linux, and Mac.
section3.queue_desc: Message queues between app components. Messages up to 64 KB. Good for decoupling.
section3.table_desc: Schemaless NoSQL key-value storage. Useful for large volumes of simple structured data.
section3.disk_desc: VM disks. Premium SSD, Standard SSD, HDD. Managed snapshots and backups.
section3.tier_hot: Hot — frequent access, higher storage cost, lower access cost.
section3.tier_cool: Cool — rarely accessed data (>30 days). Cheaper storage, pricier access.
section3.tier_archive: Archive — offline backups. Very cheap storage, but rehydration takes hours.
section3.lrs: LRS (Locally Redundant) — 3 copies in a single datacenter. Cheapest.
section3.zrs: ZRS (Zone Redundant) — copies in 3 availability zones in the same region.
section3.grs: GRS (Geo Redundant) — LRS + async replication to paired region.
section3.ragrs: RA-GRS — GRS with read enabled in the secondary region.
section3.gzrs: GZRS — ZRS + replication to paired region. Highest tier.
section3.ragzrs: RA-GZRS — GZRS with read in the secondary.
section3.azcopy: AzCopy — command-line tool to copy blobs and files. Good for automation and large volumes.
section3.stexp: Storage Explorer — GUI desktop app to manage storage (Windows, macOS, Linux).
section3.afs: Azure File Sync — syncs Azure file shares with on-premises Windows servers. Local cache.
section3.migrate: Azure Migrate — unified tool to discover, assess, and migrate servers, databases, apps, and VDI.
section3.databox: Azure Data Box — physical appliance to transfer TB/PB of data when internet is impractical. Family: Disk (up to 7TB), Box (80TB), Heavy (800TB).
section3.entraid_text: Microsoft's cloud identity directory (formerly Azure AD). Manages users, groups, applications, and devices. Identity foundation for Microsoft 365, Azure, and integrated apps.
section3.entrads_text: Managed service offering traditional Active Directory (Kerberos, NTLM, group policy) compatible with legacy apps — without managing domain controllers yourself. Useful in migrations.
section3.sso_text: Sign in once, access multiple applications. Reduces the risk of weak passwords.
section3.mfa_text: At least two factors: something you know (password), something you have (phone), something you are (biometrics).
section3.passwordless_text: Methods without passwords: Windows Hello, FIDO2 keys, Microsoft Authenticator. More secure and more convenient.
section3.external_text: Allow users from other tenants or partners to access your resources. Includes B2B Collaboration (partners) and B2C (end customers).
section3.cond_text: Set of policies that apply access controls based on signals — location, device, risk, app. E.g., 'if coming from outside the country and trying to access corporate email, require MFA.'
section3.rbac_text: Assigns permissions by role (Owner, Contributor, Reader, etc.), not by user. You assign the role to a user or group at a scope (subscription, resource group, resource). Principle of least privilege.
section3.zerotrust_text: Security model based on 'never trust, always verify.' Assumes the network may be compromised — so every request is authenticated and authorized as if it came from an open network. Three principles: verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, assume breach.
section3.dd_text: Layers of security in series — if one fails, the next still protects. Layers: data, application, compute, network, perimeter, identity/access, physical security.
section3.defender_text: CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management) + CWP (Cloud Workload Protection). Continuously assesses your security posture, detects threats, and gives recommendations with a Secure Score. Works across Azure, AWS, GCP, and on-premises.
section3.tip_html: Hierarchy: Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource. Compute types: VM (IaaS) vs App Service (PaaS) vs Functions (serverless). VPN vs ExpressRoute: VPN over public internet; ExpressRoute is dedicated private. RBAC: built-in roles + hierarchical scopes.

section4.lead: Here Azure stops being 'a bunch of services' and becomes a platform with rules: how you control costs, ensure compliance, monitor health, and manage at scale.
section4.cost_f1: Resource type — VMs cost more than queues; SQL Database costs more than Blob.
section4.cost_f2: Size/SKU — VM D8s_v4 vs B1s. Premium SSD vs Standard HDD.
section4.cost_f3: Region — some regions are pricier (especially for SQL and VMs).
section4.cost_f4: Egress traffic — inbound is free, outbound is charged (cross-region and to internet).
section4.cost_f5: Pricing model — pay-as-you-go vs reserved vs spot.
section4.cost_f6: Usage time — VMs billed per second, even when stopped (you still pay for disk storage).
section4.calc_p1: Pricing Calculator — estimates how much specific services will cost before provisioning. You select services, configure sizes, and see the monthly cost.
section4.calc_p2: TCO Calculator (Total Cost of Ownership) — compares the cost of running workloads on-premises vs Azure. Considers hardware, software, electricity, IT labor, datacenter.
section4.cm_text: Dashboard to view current spending, analyze trends, create budgets with alerts, export reports. Works at subscription or management group scope.
section4.tags_text: Key-value pairs attached to resources (e.g., 'Environment=Production', 'CostCenter=Marketing'). Allow grouping costs, organizing, and applying policies. Each resource can have up to 50 tags.
section4.purview_text: Unified platform for data governance and compliance. Catalogs data (where it lives, how sensitive), manages lifecycle, discovers information risks. Replaced Compliance Manager as the central compliance tool.
section4.policy_text: Defines rules that resources must follow (e.g., 'VMs can only be created in Brazil South and East US'). Evaluates current state and can block creations outside the rule. Assigned at hierarchical scopes.
section4.locks_text: Prevents accidental modification or deletion of critical resources. CanNotDelete: modifiable but not deletable. ReadOnly: neither modifiable nor deletable.
section4.portal_desc: Web interface to manage everything. Good for discovery, prototyping, and ad-hoc tasks.
section4.shell_desc: Browser-based terminal with Azure CLI and PowerShell preinstalled. No setup on your local machine.
section4.cli_desc: Cross-platform command line (Bash, Linux, macOS, Windows). Commands like 'az vm create...'. Good for scripts.
section4.ps_desc: PowerShell cmdlets to manage Azure (e.g., 'New-AzVM'). More verbose syntax, integrates well with Windows scripts.
section4.arc_desc: Extends Azure management to resources outside Azure — on-premises servers, other clouds, external Kubernetes. You see them as Azure resources.
section4.iac_desc: Describe infrastructure in versioned files (Git), apply as code. Guarantees reproducibility and versioning.
section4.arm_desc: The management layer behind everything in Azure — all provisioning goes through it. Defines the resource hierarchy and applies RBAC and policies.
section4.armtpl_desc: ARM templates are declarative JSON for provisioning resources. Bicep is a cleaner language that compiles to ARM. Idempotent — you can reapply without side effects.
section4.advisor_text: Personalized recommendation system across 5 categories: reliability, security, performance, cost, and operational excellence. 'You have underused VMs — consider resizing and saving X dollars.'
section4.health_text: Shows Azure service health (global incidents, planned maintenance) and how it affects your specific resources. Can be configured with alerts.
section4.monitor_text: Unified telemetry platform — metrics, logs, traces. Collects data from everything in Azure (VMs, App Service, AKS) and on-premises (via agents).
section4.monitor_la: Log Analytics — workspace to store and query logs with KQL (Kusto Query Language).
section4.monitor_alerts: Azure Monitor Alerts — rules that fire actions (email, webhook, Logic App, function) when metrics or logs cross a threshold.
section4.monitor_ai: Application Insights — APM (Application Performance Monitoring) for web apps. Shows response time, dependencies, failures, application maps.
section4.tip_html: Policy = enforces rules. Lock = prevents change/deletion. Tag = organizes/groups. Advisor = recommends. Service Health = Azure health. Monitor = telemetry. Defender = security.

section5.lead: Week-by-week roadmap using Microsoft's 4 official learning paths (free on Learn). Order matches the exam — concepts → architecture → governance → practice.
section5.week1_desc: 3 modules. Establishes the theoretical base: what cloud is, benefits, IaaS/PaaS/SaaS.
section5.week1_modules: Cloud computing · Benefits of cloud services · Cloud service types
section5.week2_title: Part 2 · Describe Azure architecture and services
section5.week2_desc: 5 modules. The largest exam block. May take 2 weeks given the number of services.
section5.week2_modules: Core architectural components · Compute · Networking · Storage · Identity, access & security
section5.week3_title: Part 3 · Describe Azure management and governance
section5.week3_desc: 4 modules. Costs, compliance, tools, and monitoring. Short but critical topics.
section5.week3_modules: Cost management · Governance and compliance · Tools to manage and deploy · Monitoring tools
section5.week4_title: Part 4 · Apply Azure skills in guided projects
section5.week4_desc: 8 guided projects, optional but highly recommended. Create a free Azure account and do real hands-on — locks in much of the abstract content.
section5.week4_modules: Static website · Tags & locks · Functions · Entra+RBAC · Secure file sharing · Cost guardrails · Monitoring · Cloud Shell + CLI
section5.key_p1_l2: Shared responsibility model (who handles what in IaaS/PaaS/SaaS)
section5.key_p1_l3: Use cases for each cloud type (public, private, hybrid)
section5.key_p2_l1: Hierarchy Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource
section5.key_p2_l2: When to use VM vs App Service vs Container vs Function
section5.key_p2_l3: VPN Gateway vs ExpressRoute (public vs dedicated private)
section5.key_p2_l5: Entra ID vs Entra Domain Services
section5.key_p2_l6: MFA, Conditional Access, RBAC, Zero Trust — distinguish each one
section5.key_p3_l1: Pricing Calculator vs TCO Calculator (estimate future vs compare to on-premises)
section5.key_p3_l2: Policy vs Lock vs Tag — what each is for
section5.key_p3_l5: Azure Arc = manage things outside Azure
